entries.meaning: A group of people working or playing together.
examples: The team is playing better than last season.
Both teams were exhausted by the fourth quarter.
She made the team on her first try.
Our team is handling the migration.
Three teams are competing for the contract.
He built a team of twelve engineers.

senses.head: A sports side
examples: The team is playing better than last season.
Both teams were exhausted by the fourth quarter.
She made the team on her first try.

senses.head: A group working together
examples: Our team is handling the migration.
Three teams are competing for the contract.
He built a team of twelve engineers.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the team is winning
entries.contrast: The team is winning is American; the team are winning is British. Both are correct in their own variety. Use the singular in American writing.

entries.meaning: A group of related people; also a taxonomic rank.
examples: My family is coming for Thanksgiving.
Three families share the building.
The whole family was at the wedding.
Oaks belong to the beech family.
Both language families are unrelated to each other.
It's a family business, now in its third generation.

senses.head: Related people
examples: My family is coming for Thanksgiving.
Three families share the building.
The whole family was at the wedding.

senses.head: A group of related things
examples: Oaks belong to the beech family.
Both language families are unrelated to each other.

senses.head: Attributive
examples: It's a family business, now in its third generation.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — my family is coming
entries.contrast: Americans say my family is coming for the holidays; the British often say are. Note that family is also a rank in biological classification, above genus.

entries.meaning: The body governing a state or organization.
examples: The government is considering new rules.
Both governments signed the treaty.
The federal government employs two million people.
Government is harder than campaigning.
She studied government and economics.

senses.head: The governing body
examples: The government is considering new rules.
Both governments signed the treaty.
The federal government employs two million people.

senses.head: The activity of governing
examples: Government is harder than campaigning.
She studied government and economics.

entries.pronunciation note: the first n is often dropped in speech
entries.agreement: singular in American English — the government is considering it
entries.contrast: ✗ The government are is British, not American. Note that the first n is commonly unpronounced — GUV-ur-muhnt — but retained in careful speech.

entries.meaning: A group appointed to decide or advise on something.
examples: The committee has decided to postpone the vote.
Both committees met the same afternoon.
She chairs the finance committee.
The committee meets on the first Monday of the month.
A camel is a horse designed by committee.

senses.head: The group
examples: The committee has decided to postpone the vote.
Both committees met the same afternoon.
She chairs the finance committee.
The committee meets on the first Monday of the month.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: A camel is a horse designed by committee.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the committee has decided
entries.contrast: Note the spelling: two m's, two t's, two e's. Stress falls on the middle syllable.

entries.meaning: A body of people sworn to give a verdict; also a panel of judges in a competition.
examples: The jury has reached a verdict.
Both juries deadlocked.
The jury were divided among themselves.
She was called for jury duty.
The jury awarded first prize unanimously.
The jury is still out on whether it works.

senses.head: In a courtroom
examples: The jury has reached a verdict.
Both juries deadlocked.
The jury were divided among themselves.
She was called for jury duty.

senses.head: A panel judging a competition
examples: The jury awarded first prize unanimously.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: The jury is still out on whether it works.

entries.agreement: usually singular in American English — the jury has reached a verdict
entries.contrast: Americans use the plural when the members are acting separately: the jury were unable to agree among themselves. When the group acts as one, singular: the jury has reached a verdict.

entries.meaning: The people watching or listening; also a formal interview.
examples: The audience was completely silent.
Both audiences reacted the same way.
She writes for a general audience.
The audience applauded for five minutes.
He was granted an audience with the ambassador.

senses.head: Spectators or listeners
examples: The audience was completely silent.
Both audiences reacted the same way.
She writes for a general audience.
The audience applauded for five minutes.

senses.head: A formal meeting with someone important
examples: He was granted an audience with the ambassador.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the audience was silent
entries.contrast: Note the separate sense 'a formal meeting with an important person', which is countable and unrelated to crowds: an audience with the pope.

entries.meaning: A large group of people gathered together.
examples: The crowd was getting restless.
Both crowds were peaceful.
A crowd had formed outside the courthouse.
She hates crowds.
He started running with a different crowd.

senses.head: A large gathering
examples: The crowd was getting restless.
Both crowds were peaceful.
A crowd had formed outside the courthouse.
She hates crowds.

senses.head: A particular social set
examples: He started running with a different crowd.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the crowd was getting restless
entries.contrast: Unlike team or committee, crowd names an unorganized group, so the plural verb is rarer even in British English.

entries.meaning: Ordinary people considered as a whole.
examples: The public is entitled to know.
The public are being asked to avoid the area.
This part of the building is closed to the public.
She has never spoken about it in public.
The museum has built a loyal public.

senses.head: People in general
examples: The public is entitled to know.
The public are being asked to avoid the area.
This part of the building is closed to the public.
She has never spoken about it in public.

senses.head: A particular set of people
examples: The museum has built a loyal public.

entries.agreement: either — the public is entitled to know / the public are being asked to stay indoors
entries.contrast: Almost always the public, never ✗ a public in this sense. American English tends to the singular verb, but the plural is common when individual people are meant.

entries.meaning: The civil force responsible for law enforcement.
examples: The police are investigating the incident.
Police have released a description.
Call the police.
Two police officers were at the door.
A police car blocked the intersection.
The police report has not been released.

senses.head: The force, or its officers
examples: The police are investigating the incident.
Police have released a description.
Call the police.
Two police officers were at the door.

senses.head: Attributive
examples: A police car blocked the intersection.
The police report has not been released.

entries.countability: plural only — no singular, no plural -s
entries.agreement: always plural — the police are investigating
entries.counted with: a police officer, two police officers
entries.contrast: ✗ The police is investigating is wrong in every variety of English, and ✗ a police for one officer is wrong too — say a police officer, a cop, or an officer. This is the one collective noun with no singular option at all.

entries.meaning: Two people together; also an approximate small number.
examples: The couple is expecting their first child.
The couple were arguing in the parking lot.
Three couples came to dinner.
A couple of people are still waiting.
It'll take a couple of days.
Give me a couple more minutes. (informal, without of)

senses.head: Two people in a relationship
examples: The couple is expecting their first child.
The couple were arguing in the parking lot.
Three couples came to dinner.

senses.head: An approximate small number
examples: A couple of people are still waiting.
It'll take a couple of days.
Give me a couple more minutes. (informal, without of)

entries.agreement: either — the couple is expecting / the couple were arguing
entries.variants: a couple of is standard; a couple without of is informal American — a couple things
entries.contrast: Two people romantically together take either verb; American English leans singular for the unit, plural when they act separately. Note that a couple of meaning 'a few' takes a plural verb: a couple of people are waiting.

entries.meaning: A quantity or figure; a quantity of things.
examples: The number of applicants is rising every year.
The number of errors was small.
A number of people are still waiting outside.
A number of problems have come up.
Pick a number between one and ten.
What's your phone number?

senses.head: the number of — a singular quantity
examples: The number of applicants is rising every year.
The number of errors was small.

senses.head: a number of — meaning 'several'
examples: A number of people are still waiting outside.
A number of problems have come up.

senses.head: A figure or numeral
examples: Pick a number between one and ten.
What's your phone number?

entries.agreement: depends on the article — the number of X is / a number of X are
entries.contrast: This is the most useful agreement rule in the language, and the two halves are exact opposites. The number of applicants is rising — one number, singular. A number of applicants are waiting — a number of just means 'several', plural. Getting this backward is one of the commonest errors in edited prose.

entries.meaning: More than half of a group.
examples: The majority of voters are undecided.
A majority of the committee were against it.
A two-thirds majority is required to amend the rules.
Her majority was just four hundred votes.
The party lost its majority in the last election.

senses.head: More than half of a group of people
body: Plural verb when of + plural noun follows. (большинство)
examples: The majority of voters are undecided.
A majority of the committee were against it.

senses.head: A margin of victory, or a required threshold
examples: A two-thirds majority is required to amend the rules.
Her majority was just four hundred votes.
The party lost its majority in the last election.

entries.agreement: depends on what follows — the majority is (as a unit) / the majority of voters are (individuals)
entries.contrast: The verb follows the noun after of. The majority of the members are opposed — plural, because members is plural. A two-thirds majority is required — singular, because it is one threshold. Same rule for minority, percentage, and half.

entries.meaning: A large group of hoofed animals.
examples: The herd is moving toward the river.
Two herds graze on the same land.
A herd of elephants crossed the road.
He keeps a herd of forty dairy cows.
She has never followed the herd.

senses.head: A group of animals
examples: The herd is moving toward the river.
Two herds graze on the same land.
A herd of elephants crossed the road.
He keeps a herd of forty dairy cows.

senses.head: A crowd of people
examples: She has never followed the herd.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the herd is moving north
entries.counted with: a herd of cattle, a herd of elephants
entries.contrast: The collective noun must match the animal: a herd of cattle, horses, elephants, deer; a flock of birds or sheep; a school of fish; a pack of wolves or dogs; a swarm of bees or insects; a pride of lions.

entries.meaning: A group of birds or sheep.
examples: A flock of geese passed overhead.
The flock is heading south early this year.
Two flocks were grazing on the hillside.
He tends a flock of two hundred sheep.
The pastor knows every member of his flock.

senses.head: A group of birds or sheep
examples: A flock of geese passed overhead.
The flock is heading south early this year.
Two flocks were grazing on the hillside.
He tends a flock of two hundred sheep.

senses.head: A congregation
examples: The pastor knows every member of his flock.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the flock is heading south
entries.counted with: a flock of birds, a flock of sheep
entries.contrast: Used of birds and of sheep, and — by extension from the shepherd metaphor — of a congregation.

entries.meaning: A large group of fish swimming together.
examples: A school of tuna passed beneath the boat.
The school is moving into deeper water.
Two schools merged into one enormous mass.
Divers filmed a school of hammerheads.
Small fish form schools for protection.

senses.head: A group of fish
examples: A school of tuna passed beneath the boat.
The school is moving into deeper water.
Two schools merged into one enormous mass.
Divers filmed a school of hammerheads.
Small fish form schools for protection.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the school is moving away from the boat
entries.contrast: Unrelated to the educational sense despite the identical spelling — this school comes from a Dutch word meaning 'crowd'. The related term shoal means the same thing.

entries.meaning: A large group of insects moving together.
examples: A swarm of bees settled in the chimney.
The swarm is heading for the orchard.
Two swarms left the hive that week.
Swarms of locusts destroyed the crop.
A swarm of reporters met him at the airport.

senses.head: A mass of insects
examples: A swarm of bees settled in the chimney.
The swarm is heading for the orchard.
Two swarms left the hive that week.
Swarms of locusts destroyed the crop.

senses.head: A crowd of people
examples: A swarm of reporters met him at the airport.

entries.agreement: singular in American English — the swarm is moving toward the orchard
entries.counted with: a swarm of bees, a swarm of insects
entries.contrast: Used of insects, and figuratively of any fast-moving mass of people.
